subject: giraffe
pitch: A young reticulated giraffe. Chestnut patches outlined by bright cream lines all over its body and neck, a short mane of stiff brown hair down the neck, two fuzzy ossicones with black tufts on top, big ears, long lashes, a long dark tongue just peeking out, and slender legs fading to cream above the hooves.
reasoning:
I'm working within the SDK's known API surface, aiming for something correct and runnable. Now I'm sketching proportions for a young giraffe model — scaling shoulder and head height against adult size, with body length around 1.4m and legs around 1m.

Mapping out the skeleton next: hip joint height, leg segment lengths down to the hoof, and a spine chain running from tail base to withers, then a forward-sloping neck up to the head. I'm planning to build the torso as a sweep along a path between tail and chest, checking how the SDK's chain function lays joints along that curve.

For coloring, I'm weighing uncertain APIs like paint, spots, stripes, and decals against safer bets like plain sweeps and surfaces, since I'm not fully sure of their exact signatures and want to avoid relying on guessed behavior.

For the chestnut patches, I'll fake the reticulated look by stacking flattened spheres directly on the body surface — a larger cream sphere slightly behind a smaller chestnut sphere on top, both scaled flat and seated using the surface's nearest-point hit so they conform to the body.

I'm scattering patch positions across the surface using random sampling fed through nearest-point projection for determinism, then sticking each flattened sphere geometry onto its hit frame, though I'm unsure exactly which local axis the stick function aligns to the surface normal.

For the ossicones, I'm sketching stems as capsules or cylinders topped with small black spheres, considering whether sprout or spike functions are the right primitives to grow these sub-parts from the head.

For ears, legs, and joints, I'm leaning toward relying on b.part with `at` and `dir` for consistent alignment, using flattened ellipsoid shapes for the ears and planning joint names like hipL/kneeL/ankleL for each leg chain.

For the body, I'm thinking a capsule aligned along the Z-axis works best, positioned at the torso center with the "hips" bone as its anchor, plus maybe a separate sphere for the chest—though I still need to figure out how patches/texturing would apply across these pieces.

Actually, switching approach: I'll build the body and neck as sweeps along spine paths with roughly constant radii for a stylized look, then wrap surfaces around them for patch application. The head will be a scaled sphere plus a boxy muzzle, jointed at the top of the neck.

For facial details I'm placing a dark tongue, eyes with small lash-like boxes angled outward, and for the mane I'm sticking tiny brown cone shapes along the top ridge of the neck to suggest short stiff hair.

I'm computing neck centerline positions manually with piecewise linear interpolation so the hair points surface correctly, then adding ossicones as small cylinders topped with black spheres near the head crown. Next I'll generate randomized body patch positions by sampling points along the body's path and wrapping them around the surface.

Writing patch stacking code...

Now I'm settling on a color palette: chestnut browns for patches, cream/fawn tones for the body and outlines, dark brown-black for hooves, mane, and tongue, with legs transitioning from chestnut upper to cream lower near the hooves.

I'm sketching ear geometry and placement — small flattened spheres positioned near the head, oriented directly in model space rather than relying on directional aiming, since I'm unsure how the aim-to-bone system handles non-vertical limbs. I'm also checking that the overall part count from patches, mane, and other details stays well under limits, and deciding to reuse geometries across stick calls where possible for efficiency.

For the patch placement itself, I'm accepting that symmetric sphere geometry sidesteps uncertainty about normal-to-axis mapping, flattening along one axis to keep patches hugging the surface regardless of how orientation gets resolved.

For the neck and spine, I'm keeping it simple by using a sweep along a path without a tied chain, letting bone skinning fall to the nearest joint automatically, then rigging joints for the hips and spine separately.

Rather than chaining, I'll set up explicit joints for the neck segments and head, each parented to the previous one up through hips, with coordinates given in absolute model-space positions matching the spec's example. Then I'm working out the leg joint hierarchy, placing hip, knee, and ankle joints parented successively from the hips root.

For the leg geometry, since legs run roughly vertical I can use default-oriented cylinders without worrying about custom alignment -- building upper and lower leg segments with tapered cylinder geometry, small sphere joints at the knees, and hoof caps at the ankles, fading color from chestnut tan near the hip to a cream tone lower down.

Now I'm mapping out the tail as a swept path with a dark tuft sphere at the tip, the body as a thin horizontal sweep, and the neck as a tapering sweep curving upward from the body to the head joint. For the head, I'm placing a boxy skull and muzzle plus a small dark nose block positioned relative to the head joint coordinates.

Adding facial details...

For mane bristles, I'm computing points along the neck surface using sweep geometry and sticking cone shapes outward along the normal direction so they stand up naturally off the skin. For body patches, I'm scattering random points across the body and neck surfaces using spherical directions, then projecting them onto the nearest surface point to place patches, making sure the normal faces outward correctly.

For coloring, I'm settling on a tan/fawn base body color with bright cream outlines and chestnut-colored patches to mimic a reticulated giraffe's coat pattern, layering the patches slightly above the surface so the cream rings and chestnut centers stand out visually.

I'm now working through the full rig: joints for shoulders, knees, and ankles on each leg, cylinder geometries for upper/lower leg segments and hooves sized so the leg bottoms meet the ground at y=0, and a body sweep with randomly scattered patch pairs (chestnut centers outlined in cream) projected onto the body and neck surfaces via nearest-point lookups. I'm also adding a mane of small cones along the neck ridge, ossicones with dark tufts on the head, a boxy skull and muzzle, eyes with eyelash details made from thin rotated boxes, and planning ear geometry next -- aiming for roughly 250 total parts while keeping proportions consistent with a young giraffe around 3.3–3.8 units tall.

Now I'm figuring out ear shape, tongue, tail, and jaw placement: scaling sphere geometry asymmetrically to make flat, wide ears positioned on the sides of the head, using a capsule rotated along the Z-axis for the tongue, a tapering sweep path for the tail with a dark tuft at the tip, and a separate jaw joint parented to the head so the mouth can be built as distinct upper and lower parts. I'm settling on creation order -- joints first (hips, neck, head, jaw), then the leg loop, then body/neck sweeps and surface patches -- and deciding to stick with explicit joints rather than chains for simplicity before writing out the final assembled code and meta export.
